title: 7 Christmas Card Mistakes That Send Yours Straight to the TRASH

scenes.text: Sweetheart, I have a shoebox in my closet with every Christmas card my mother ever kept. Over four hundred of them, from nineteen forty-six to nineteen ninety-seven. And here's what I noticed when I went through them. She threw away the store-bought ones with just a signature. She kept every single one where somebody had written a few real words, by hand.
scenes.caption: SHE KEPT EVERY ONE

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you seven Christmas card mistakes that send your card straight to the trash, and how to write one that people keep for fifty years. And stay with me, because the last one is the card that matters most, and it's the one almost nobody sends anymore.
scenes.caption: STRAIGHT TO THE TRASH

scenes.text: In our house on Elm Street, Christmas cards were a big event. My mother bought a box of fifty at Woolworth's the day after Thanksgiving, and she wrote them at the kitchen table every evening for a week, with her good fountain pen. Every card got a real note. And when the cards came in, she taped them around the doorway to the front room, so the door was framed in Christmas.
scenes.caption: A WEEK OF EVENINGS

scenes.text: The mailman came twice a day in December back then, honey. Morning and afternoon. Danny and I ran to the mailbox every time, and we fought over who got to open them. Getting a card meant somebody, somewhere, sat down and thought of you. In a minute I'll tell you the first mistake, and it's the one that makes a card feel like a bill.
scenes.caption: TWICE A DAY

scenes.text: Mistake number one. Just a signature. A printed card that says Merry Christmas, signed Bob and Linda, with nothing else. It takes three seconds to read and one second to throw away. The fix is simple. Write at least two or three sentences by hand. That's all. Not a letter. Just a few real words for that one person.
scenes.caption: JUST A SIGNATURE

scenes.text: Here's my rule, sweetheart. Every card gets one memory and one wish. One memory. I still think about the Christmas Eve we sang carols on your porch in nineteen seventy-eight. And one wish. I hope your new knee lets you dance at your granddaughter's wedding. That's three sentences, and the person will read it four times.
scenes.caption: ONE MEMORY, ONE WISH

scenes.text: Mistake number two. The long typed newsletter all about how wonderful your year was. Johnny made the honor roll, Susie won the piano competition, and we took a lovely cruise to Alaska. People call them brag letters, honey, and they groan when they open them. If you send a letter, keep it to one page, be honest, include the funny parts and the hard parts, and ask about them.
scenes.caption: THE BRAG LETTER

scenes.text: My friend Joyce sent the best Christmas letter I ever read, in nineteen eighty-four. It said, this year the roof leaked, the dog ate the Thanksgiving turkey, Harold had his gallbladder out, and we have never been happier to be alive. We miss you. Come visit. Everybody on her list kept that letter. I read it every December, and I still laugh.
scenes.caption: THE DOG ATE THE TURKEY

scenes.text: Mistake number three. Printed address labels and a printed return address. It looks like a bill or an advertisement. People open the bills last. Address the envelope by hand. And use a real stamp, a Christmas stamp if you can, not a machine postage strip. An envelope with handwriting and a pretty stamp is the first one people open from the whole pile of mail.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST ONE OPENED

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. And a little trick my mother used. Tuck something small and flat inside the card. A pressed sprig of pine. A paper snowflake. A little photo. A recipe card. A child's drawing. It makes opening it feel like opening a tiny present.
scenes.caption: A TINY PRESENT

scenes.text: Mistake number four. Sending them too late, on the twenty-third, so they arrive after Christmas, with the bills and the after-Christmas sales. Mail your cards in the first two weeks of December. That way, people have time to enjoy them, hang them up and set them on the mantel. And send them early to anybody overseas, by the end of November.
scenes.query: mailbox full Christmas cards early December
scenes.caption: THE FIRST TWO WEEKS

scenes.text: So far, write a few real words, skip the brag letter, address it by hand, and mail it early. And here's how to make it easy, sweetheart. Do five cards a night, like my mother did, with a cup of tea and some carols on the radio. Fifty cards is ten quiet evenings. It's one of the nicest parts of December, if you don't try to do them all at once.
scenes.caption: FIVE A NIGHT

scenes.text: And keep a list, honey. A little notebook, or a page in your address book, with every name, the address, and a check mark for the years you sent a card and the years you got one. My mother's list goes back to nineteen forty-six, in pencil, with names crossed out and new babies added. It's the history of our whole family, in one little book. When someone moves, write the new address right away.
scenes.caption: KEEP A LIST

scenes.text: Mistake number five. The exact same message in every card. People compare, honey. Your sister and your aunt will put them side by side on the kitchen counter and notice. Write something different for each person, even if it's short. Mention their garden, their new grandbaby, their dog, the pie they brought to the picnic. Specific is what makes it feel personal.
scenes.query: two identical cards side by side
scenes.caption: PEOPLE COMPARE

scenes.text: Mistake number six. A photo card with nothing written on it. Family photo cards are lovely. I keep every one of my grandchildren's. But a photo with only a printed greeting is like a smile with no hello. Turn it over and write a few words on the back by hand. Even one line. Thinking of you, Aunt Ruth, the twins are finally sleeping through the night.
scenes.caption: A SMILE WITH NO HELLO

scenes.text: And date it, sweetheart. Write the year on the back of every photo card you keep, in pen. In forty years, your grandchildren won't know if that baby in the Santa hat is their father or their uncle. My mother wrote the names and the year on every photo card. Thanks to her, I know exactly who everybody is in a box of four hundred cards.
scenes.query: writing year on back of photo
scenes.caption: DATE IT

scenes.text: And now mistake number seven, the card that matters most, the one almost nobody sends anymore. Forgetting the people who are alone. The widow down the street. The old teacher. Your mother's old friend in the nursing home. The neighbor whose husband died this year. For them, a Christmas card might be the only mail they get all December.
scenes.caption: THE PEOPLE WHO ARE ALONE

scenes.text: When my husband passed, in two thousand eleven, I got a card from a boy I'd taught in Sunday school in nineteen seventy-two. He was sixty years old by then. He wrote, Mrs. Ruth, you taught me the Christmas story with a flannel board and a box of animal crackers, and I've told it to my own children every year since. I put that card on my nightstand, and it's still there.
scenes.caption: IT'S STILL THERE

scenes.text: So this year, honey, add five people to your list who aren't expecting a card from you. And if you can, write something they'll want to keep. Tell them what they meant to you. People wait their whole lives to hear it, and most of them never do. A card is the easiest way in the world to say it.
scenes.caption: TELL THEM

scenes.text: And don't forget the children, sweetheart. Children almost never get real mail. Send a card to each grandchild, niece and nephew, addressed to them by name, not to their parents. Put a dollar bill or a sheet of stickers inside. Danny's grandson told me my card was the only mail he got all year with his own name on it. He's twelve, and he answered with a letter. In pencil.
scenes.query: child opening card with own name
scenes.caption: THEIR OWN NAME

scenes.text: And when the cards come in, display them, sweetheart. Tape them around a doorway like my mother did. Hang them on a ribbon across the mantel with little clothespins. Or put them in a big basket by the sofa, so visitors can look through them. And after Christmas, keep the ones that matter in a box. In fifty years, that box will be a treasure.
scenes.query: Christmas cards hung on ribbon clothespins
scenes.caption: A TREASURE IN FIFTY YEARS

scenes.text: And the rest, honey, cut out the pretty fronts and use them as gift tags next year, like I told you before. Or let the grandchildren cut them up for crafts. My mother made a little Christmas card quilt from the fronts, glued onto cardboard and laced together with yarn. It hung in our kitchen for twenty years.
scenes.caption: A CHRISTMAS CARD QUILT

scenes.text: And if you're short on money for cards and stamps this year, honey, there's no shame in it. Make them. Fold a piece of plain paper, draw a little tree, or let the children draw. Or send an email or a text with a real message and a photo. The rule is the same. A few real words, written for one person. That's what people keep, not the paper.
scenes.caption: MAKE THEM

scenes.text: So one more time. Write a few real words, one memory and one wish. Skip the brag letter, or make it honest and funny. Address it by hand, with a real stamp. Mail it early. Write something different for each person. Write on the back of the photo, and date it. And send a card to somebody who's alone. That's how to write a Christmas card people keep for fifty years.
scenes.caption: KEPT FOR FIFTY YEARS

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Do you still send Christmas cards? And what's the best one you ever got? I'd love to hear about it. The whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. Merry Christmas.
scenes.caption: THE BEST CARD YOU GOT?
